 OPINION: Daylight saving time has outlived its usefulness
 Kayla Lucas , Correspondent 
 • 
 Nov 19, 2026 
 Avery McIver, Graphic Illustrator 
 Every year, Americans participate in changing the clocks. We lose an hour, mess up our sleep schedules and then go on as if it’s a perfectly reasonable way to organize society. 
 At some point, we have to ask ourselves: Why are we still doing this? 
 Daylight saving was originally implemented in the U.S. in 1918 during World War I as a way to conserve energy. The idea was to change daylight hours to make better use of natural sunlight and also reduce the need for artificial lighting. 
 After the war, the practice stopped, but then started again in 1942 during World War II, followed by standardization through the Uniform Act of 1966 . In 2005, Congress extended the daylight saving period, creating the schedule we follow today. 
 Why am I telling you all of this? Because I want to make the point that daylight saving time did, at some point in history, serve a real purpose. It was introduced in response to the circumstances at the time, and there was a practical reason behind it. 
 But circumstances have changed, and policies should be able to change with them. Just because something made sense in 1918 does not mean it makes sense in 2026. 
 And that’s exactly where my argument begins: Daylight saving time has outlived its usefulness. 
 For starters, changing the clocks disrupts routines that people often spend the rest of the year trying to maintain. Sleep schedules, work schedules and daily responsibilities don’t suddenly become more flexible just because time changes. 
 Losing an hour of sleep in a random month of the year is just treated like a minor inconvenience, something we complain about for maybe a day or two, but then we move on. 
 But sleep is not something we can adjust at the snap of a finger. Our bodies require and rely on a consistent sleep pattern, and changing that randomly throws those patterns off. 
 Why are we even voluntarily making that disruption? Don’t we already have enough reasons in the day to lose sleep without daylight saving time being added to the list? 
 But let’s not stop there. My biggest issue with daylight saving time isn’t even the lost hour of sleep. 
 It’s walking out of class at 5:00 p.m. and realizing the sun has already set. 
 During the colder months, daylight becomes increasingly limited, and for people who spend most of their day working or attending classes, the opportunity to enjoy it is even smaller. 
 By the time people finish their daily responsibilities, it’s already dark and cold outside. 
 All of a sudden, going on a walk, exercising outdoors and meeting up with friends feels like another task to squeeze into a busy schedule. Instead of feeling like there is still a day to enjoy, it feels like the day is over before it really begins. 
 We talk about the importance of being outside, staying active and taking care of our mental health, particularly during the winter months. Yet, currently, our schedule makes it harder for people with traditional work and school schedules to take advantage of the daylight they do have. 
 It’s difficult to encourage people to spend more time outside when they leave their classrooms and workplaces to find that the sun has already gone down. 
 We have spent more than a century adjusting our lives around daylight saving time; maybe it’s time to question why. Our schedules have changed, our lifestyles have changed, and the original circumstances that justified the practice are no longer relevant. 
 Continuing to change the clocks because we’ve always done it is not a convincing reason to keep doing it. 
 I’m not asking for more hours in the day. I’m asking for the hours we already have to feel like they’re worth something. People should be able to finish a day of work and still have time to enjoy the daylight instead of feeling like their free time begins after the sun has already disappeared. 
 We don’t need to keep treating a century-old policy as a permanent part of American life. It’s time to stop changing the clocks.
